MAHA PAC spent more on steak, luxury club than candidates, report shows

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals.
  • The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.
  • According to recent reports, the findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA’s own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group’s priority was ever winning elections in the first place.

The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.

According to recent reports, the findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.

According to Stat’s findings, of the $10.5 million the MAHA PAC spent on the midterms, less than a tenth—roughly $1 million—went to messaging on political candidates, which are expenses called “independent expenditures.”.

Andrew Mayersohn, a committees researcher at OpenSecrets, called the spending “pretty unusual,” explaining that “Major super PACs spend most of their money on independent expenditures.”.

In some cases, the scant political spending was dwarfed by spending on luxuries. For instance, in a key House race in Northern California, MAHA supported Kevin Kiley over his political rival, pediatrician Richard Pan. Despite calling the race “the most direct ideological confrontation” between MAHA and its opposition “anywhere on the 2026 ballot,” the PAC only spent $49,900 to back Kiley. That’s a little less than the $50,100 it spent at Mastro’s Steakhouse, an upscale restaurant that offers $110 porterhouse steaks in Washington, DC. Further, it’s less than a third of the $155,900 the PAC spent at Ned’s Club, a luxury club near the White House that has become a popular gathering spot among Trump officials.

Kiley lost the election to Pan by double digits.

Of the roughly $1 million spent on political candidates, most of it—over $700,000—went to defeating Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.). Many other MAHA-endorsed candidates received $50,000 or less. Some got less than $2,000.

Outside of steaks and a private club, the MAHA PAC spent $500,000 on a media company, Merit Street Media, run by Phil McGraw, who hosted a MAHA special featuring Dr. Phil. MAHA leaders used PAC money to cover meals, payroll, and credit card bills. The PAC paid $275,000 to a security firm, Gavin de Becker & Associates, which is led by an ally of anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., MAHA’s top leader. Tens of thousands more went to LLCs that have little to no online information.

On the other hand, prominent online MAHA influencers also pocketed tens of thousands from the PAC, as did writers for The MAHA Report, a Substack that promotes Kennedy and MAHA interests. In the days after the midterms, as members of the movement were coming to grips with the election losses, The MAHA Report chose to publish a lengthy article defending convicted rapist Russel Brand, a Kennedy ally who became a MAHA fixture.

According to recent reports, the biggest chunk of the MAHA PAC’s spending—more than $3 million—went to the nonprofit MAHA Action, which is also run by Lyons. It’s unclear how all that money was spent.

Tech Report: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charity that collects the coins indicates donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access.
  • According to recent reports, when Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it.
  • He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charity that collects the coins indicates donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access.

According to recent reports, when Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” mentioned Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.

He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

But the only thing holding him back from partaking in the gesture was the distance: the steps towards the fountain’s sunken basin are separated by a low barrier and accessible during the day only by Rome’s residents or visitors who pay €2 (£1.64).

Sources indicate that the fee, in place since February, has been partly blamed for taking some of the allure out of the coin-throwing tradition. The Rome unit of the church-run charity Caritas, which sweeps up the Trevi fountain’s coins, usually brings in more than €1.4m a year. But it noted a shortfall of about €200,000 between January and September compared with the same period in 2025.

According to recent reports, “The closure of the direct access to the Trevi fountain might be a factor,” Giustino Trincia, the director of Caritas Roma, told Il Messaggero. The charity uses the donations to fund food banks and other welfare projects.

Clinton did contemplate asking someone in the basin area to throw the coin into the fountain on his behalf, but in the end slipped it back into his pocket.

The shift towards contactless payments and mobile phone wallets is also believed to have eroded Caritas’s collections.

Recent findings suggest that eric and Patty, a young couple from Latest York, mentioned they might have thrown a coin, but did not have any change. Neither did they want to pay the €2 fee to get close to the basin. “It’s such a breathtaking monument, we’re happy just to take it in from here,” said Patty as they posed for selfies.

Alan and Ying, visiting Rome from Australia, did pay the fee. While they had heard that throwing coins “is what people do”, they decided not to indulge because “nobody else was really doing it”.

According to recent reports, “I always carry cash with me because you never know when you might need it,” stated Ying. “But we didn’t see anyone else doing it, so we didn’t either.”.

A spokesperson for Caritas Rome told the Guardian the charity was not making any further public statements about the dwindling coin collection. The spokesperson stated the collection so far this year did not take into account foreign currency coins, so the hit might not be so bad.

Still, the matter is understood to have caused friction with Rome’s council, which generated €435,194 from the access fee within the first month of its inception.

Sources indicate that the initiative is aimed at curbing overcrowding at the monument while raising funds for the upkeep of the fountain and other Rome monuments. No further figures have been published, but with 4.4 million tourists flocking to the Trevi in 2025, the fee had been forecast to generate a tidy income for the council each year.

A team of stewards staff the ticketing system and monitor the flow of the crowd in the basin area. Nicolas Romero does shifts of seven or eight hours. He mentioned people quite often asked him for change in order to throw a coin. “But many don’t even seem to know about the tradition,” he said. “This might also explain the decline.”.

The gesture is believed to have its origins in an ancient pagan ritual offering to the water gods, although the custom of throwing coins only really took off globally after the 1954 romantic comedy film, Three Coins in the Fountain.

Best Power Banks (2026): My Picks After Testing Over 100

📅 31 Jan 2021 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve.
  • Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options.
  • Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.

Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.

Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

Recent findings suggest that this is the only power bank you need. Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.

OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights, so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any issues. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.

It has been revealed that you don’t always need substantial capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy new range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.

Sources indicate that another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts. Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.

The original was the first Qi2 power bank I tested and was my top pick for quite a while, but this sequel is even better. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. Because it works with Apple's StandBy mode, you can stick Qi2 or MagSafe phones in portrait or landscape orientation.

Recent findings suggest that qi2 brings faster wireless charging rates of up to 25 watts, but it is also backward compatible, so older Qi devices can still charge (albeit more slowly). This compact portable charger has a handy kickstand, a two-way USB-C port on the left edge, and a power button with an LED display that can show remaining power as a percentage. It can also display charging time when plugged in, watts out, temperature, and battery health. Anker offers the device in a range of fun colors (I love the burgundy). Anker has added vents on top and bottom with a cooling fan you can turn off for silent mode. It is slimmer and lighter than the original and can charge faster, but it's also more expensive.

Sources indicate that despite a large capacity, it falls short of two full charges for your iPhone when charging wirelessly. You might squeeze out a little more if you plug in the short USB-C cable provided. It’s also quite bulky, but if you have an iPhone or another Qi2 phone, we recommend several slimmer alternatives in our Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks guide.

Maybe you want a large-capacity power bank that can handle all your portable gadgets, but you’re tired of gray bricks. I am a sucker for Sharge’s transparent designs and cyberpunk aesthetic, but this prism-shaped power bank is more than just a pretty face. With a maximum output of 170 watts, a whopping 24,000-mAh capacity, and an IP66 rating for water resistance (fine in the rain, but best not to submerge), the Sharge 170 has form and function. The smart display shows battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts. It supports many standards, including Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, and it fast-charged most of the devices I tested, including the iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, Xiaomi 14 Ultra, and MacBook Air. You can simultaneously charge three devices at fast speeds.

In a recent development, the box includes a braided USB-C cable and a somewhat pointless wee velvety bag (does anyone use these?). It can recharge completely in an hour via USB-C at up to 140 watts (with the right cable and charger). I’ve tested some of Sharge’s newer power banks, but I still prefer the 170. The triangular design is unique and means the display is always angled perfectly to glance at. You are paying a premium for the aesthetic, but I’ve used mine often over the last few months. It’s built to last.

My Apple Watch usually makes it to bedtime, but for super busy days and overnight trips, it’s nice to have a power bank capable of charging it up. This Anker power bank has a handy pop-up Apple Watch charger that can deliver 5 watts and supports Nightstand mode. It also has a built-in USB-C cable and a USB-C port, so you can deliver up to 30 watts to your phone or another small device. A display lights up beneath the surface to show you the remaining power as a percentage, and the current charging rate. It’s nice and compact, with a generous 10,000-mAh battery capacity, and comes in black, white, green, or pink. Anker supplies stickers to stop your Apple Watch from sliding, but I didn’t find that to be a problem.

Innovative and genuinely useful, I love the Nimble SharePower, a 10,000-mAh, modular power bank that you can snap in half to get two separate, fully functional 5,000-mAh chargers. This clever design allows you to share power with friends and family. The two halves connect magnetically with tiny pogo pins (it’s satisfying to pull them apart and reconnect). One has a built-in USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop, and the other has a fold-out USB-C connector. Put them together, and the remaining power is split evenly between the two halves. My daughter pinched this soon after it arrived in my home because it enables her to share the power with her friends, and I’m having trouble getting it back.

It has been revealed that there are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks, Best MagSafe Power Banks, and Best Portable Power Stations.

According to recent reports, with its lovely textured finish and sleek design, this magnetic Qi2 power bank is a looker. It sticks to the back of your phone and charges wirelessly at 15 watts, also doubling as a stand for travel, thanks to its sturdy aluminum kickstand. When you plug it in via USB-C, it supports 25-watt wireless charging for your phone and pass-through charging, so it charges the battery at the same time. It has four LEDs and a power button on the bottom edge. On the downside, it’s expensive and doesn't come with a cable or power adapter.

According to recent reports, super svelte, about the same size as a stack of credit cards, this charger slides easily into pockets and bags and offers a modest top-up for your phone. The USB-C connector pops out, and it comes in loads of colors.

Anker’s dinky charger comes in fun colors and simply slots into the bottom of your phone via the built-in rotating USB-C or Lightning connector. It charges at 22.5 watts and has four LEDs to show remaining power.

This wafer-thin Qi2 power bank clings to the back of your phone magnetically for up to 15-watt wireless charging, providing enhanced safety and reduced fire risk. There's also a chunkier 10,000-mAh model with a handy display.

Recent findings suggest that how slim can a MagSafe power bank get? This one is just 0.27 inches, the thinnest I’ve tested, and it sticks to the back of your iPhone (or Qi2 Android phone) magnetically. It only charges at 7.5 watts, but using the tiny, braided USB-C cable can boost it up to 22.5 watts. The NFC app connection to show exact remaining power was flaky in my testing, but it’s not required to use. If you don’t mind something slightly thicker (0.5 inches), you can double the capacity and get Qi2 charging with the next model up ($70), but both are frequently discounted, so don’t pay full price.

This svelte, lightweight, 15,000-mAh power bank has a color display for stats and can deliver 65 watts across up to three devices. It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A, is fast to recharge (around 90 minutes at 100 watts), supports most fast-charging protocols and trickle charging for small devices, and is CCC certified for trips to China.

This model has a 2.3-foot retractable cable and the ability to charge devices at up to 45 watts.

Handmade by a small indie business in Brighton, England, from recycled plastic, Gomi claims at least 50 percent less CO2 emissions than other power banks.

It’s not fast, but this 10,000-mAh power bank has built-in USB-C and Lightning cables, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a handy display.

This is an affordable 20,000-mAh-capacity power bank with a cable that doubles as a carry loop. The USB-C cable and port can deliver a maximum of 67 watts (PD), and the USB-A can hit 22.5 watts, but those speeds drop if you charge multiple devices at once. It won’t fast-charge everything, and you won’t get the full capacity stated, but it’s a pretty good value.

Capable of delivering 300 watts, this power bank is close to the maximum capacity allowed on flights, and it can charge a couple of laptops and phones at the same time via the three USB-C ports (140W, 65W, 65W) and a retractable 2-foot USB-C cable (140W).

Looking like a power bank from the Nostromo, this can deliver a chart-topping 240 watts for two devices via the USB-C ports (140 watts and 100 watts), making it a good choice if you want to charge two laptops simultaneously.

Feature-packed with 26,250 mAh at 300 watts across two USB-C ports and one USB-A, a smart display and app control, and a 3.3-foot USB-C cable, this Anker Prime Power Bank is a beast.

Travel plug adapters cover trips to the UK, Europe, and Australia, among other places. It also has three ports and a magnetic Qi2 wireless charging pad.

You get slide-on Type C, I, and G plug adapters for travel, a magnetic wireless charger (up to 15 watts), USB-A and USB-C ports, and built-in USB-C and Lightning cables.

After extensive testing, this is our pick of the best portable jump starters, and it can charge gadgets at up to 65 watts via USB-C.

Small but mighty, this 10,000 mAh power bank is shock-, water-, and dustproof with an IP67 rating. A flap covers two USB-C ports, and there’s a ¼-inch thread for mounting—or you can screw in the supplied D-ring and use the carabiner to attach it to your bag. There’s even a small flashlight you can switch on by double-pressing the power button. It comes with a short braided USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop.

Thoughtfully designed power banks with an IP67 rating, built-in shock absorbers, and screw-on caps for the ports.

This portable charger has a whopping 90,000-mAh capacity, a pop-up lantern, and a versatile array of ports.

The Charge 100 Max can simultaneously charge up to five devices, and the wireless charging pad on top is handy in the dark when you don’t want to fumble with cables.

Industry observers note that interesting and innovative, this magnetic power bank doubles as a camera grip with a built-in Bluetooth shutter button. There’s also a display showing how much of the 9,300-mAh capacity remains, a retractable USB-C cable, and a tripod thread.

It has been revealed that this compact carbon fiber Nitecore power bank is the lightest I’ve tested with a 10,000-mAh capacity. It weighs just 5 ounces (143 grams), and it scores an IPX7 rating, meaning it’s rain- and splash-proof. If you’re a trail runner or keen hiker, this could be your perfect power bank. I like the light-up USB-C ports, brought to life by the touch-sensitive power button, making it easy to plug in when it’s dark. The tradeoff to keep the weight down is that it’s relatively slow (no heat sink). You can expect a 15-watt charging rate, though it can recharge at up to 22.5 watts. It comes with a tiny USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop.

These portable chargers I tested aren’t necessarily terrible, but you can do better.

UGreen MagFlow Pro for $90: I actually quite like this magnetic, wireless charging power bank (Qi2 25W) with its Matrix-style screen that animates to show charging status. But considering the 10,000-mAh capacity, the price is absolutely bonkers. The marketing talks up its cooling properties, but it got very warm when I used it. The attached USB-C cable (45W) was annoyingly obtrusive when it was stuck to the back of my iPhone.

OnePlus Slim Magnetic Power Bank for $70: Sleek in silver-gray aluminum with a chamfered edge, this power bank looks lovely, but the 5,000-mAh capacity is just over half that after inefficiency takes a bite.

Recent findings suggest that iniu Portable Charger for $20: It’s very small for a 10,000-mAh capacity. You can charge at up to 45 watts from either of the USB-C ports or 18 watts from the USB-A (recharging was slow), it fell short of the stated capacity, and the display sometimes failed to update correctly.

FansDreams MChaos for $46: I love the idea of a wearable power bank, and this one comes in lime green with a carabiner that makes it easy to attach to a bag, but recharging is slow, and you’ll be lucky to get one full charge for your phone. It's also at the moment sold out.

iWalk Portable Charger for $22: The 4,800-mAh capacity won’t come close to fully refilling your device, but it's tiny enough to keep in a bag at all times.

What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no issues. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

It has been revealed that some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks.

Industry observers note that many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

It has been revealed that the chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:.

Recent findings suggest that avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most key rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

Recent findings suggest that I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

Industry observers note that I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (currently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Industry observers note that aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown latest brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something upcoming if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
  • According to recent reports, "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say.

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

According to recent reports, "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she indicates. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life.".

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city.

It has been revealed that on streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Industry observers note that estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Sources indicate that some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

Industry observers note that "Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

Sources indicate that "It used to be a lively city," she states. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous.".

She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she indicates.

Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade.

It has been revealed that war is not fresh to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

According to recent reports, houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

Sources indicate that in recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he indicates. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him.".

Recent findings suggest that most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", claims Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says.

If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," notes Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.

"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he notes. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents.".

We have not been able to independently verify these figures.

According to recent reports, he remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

According to recent reports, he tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

According to recent reports, the Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, indicates Shamsan.

He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

Sources indicate that "Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

How long can the city hold out, I ask.

"Until the population perishes," he replies.

Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Industry observers note that akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (Â£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

He tells us this fight is different to 2015.

Sources indicate that "This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he claims. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves.".

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He notes that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the glitch) but not by the UK or the European Union.

Industry observers note that "They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," notes Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city.".

Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months.

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes.".

The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us.".

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

But could they fight their way in?

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party.".

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports.".

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor.

It has been revealed that rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father stated as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

In a recent development, she studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she mentioned.

According to recent reports, rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

It has been revealed that "They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method.".

It has been revealed that rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), mentioned Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us.".

Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website.
  • Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a Latest York City bill.

Sources indicate that I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for customers of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged in to Amazon.

Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:.

In a recent development, right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is newly introduced is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

It has been revealed that the messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any tech giant with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

Sources indicate that it also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other challenges. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up reveals Amazon extending that strategy directly to its owners.

In a recent development, given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

Finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

The Delivery Protection Act is currently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

    • GTA+ adds a few perks to GTA 6 and one of them is already stirring up players.
    • A lot has changed in gaming in the 13 years since Grand Theft Auto 5 debuted.
    • That $8 gets you a few perks in GTA 6, but nothing game-changing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA+ adds a few perks to GTA 6 and one of them is already stirring up players.

    A lot has changed in gaming in the 13 years since Grand Theft Auto 5 debuted. That includes the explosion of live-service games and gaming subscriptions, and the Grand Theft Auto franchise has gotten in on both with GTA Online and the GTA+ membership. Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is out, GTA+ members get some additional benefits in the newly introduced game on top of what the subscription already offers in GTA Online.

    That $8 gets you a few perks in GTA 6, but nothing game-changing. You'll get 10 percent more money for any eligible vehicles you sell in the game and a 10 percent discount at a variety of stores. You can also use in-game transport options like scooters, bikes and public transit for free and get a premium membership to the RydeMe rideshare service. Together, those perks add up to a few cheaper ways to get around GTA 6's huge map and an easier time making cash. That can make a substantial difference in your progress early in the game, since cheats don't unlock until you beat the story.

    The biggest and most controversial benefit is one you can claim only after reaching GTA 6's third chapter. At that point, you'll get the '90 Annis Venturas BLVD Elegy, a free sports car, plus a garage in the Crosstown area. Locking exclusive items in a single-player game behind a monthly subscription is never popular, and players have already voiced their displeasure on Reddit.

    For most players, the GTA+ subscription fee probably isn't worth it for what it adds to GTA 6 alone. From the start, GTA+ has focused mostly on GTA Online, giving members in-game currency and discounts, new vehicles and garages to store them in, and a rotating suite of items and features. For dedicated GTA Online players who also picked up GTA 6, there's a much better case for the subscription.

    According to recent reports, the game library included with GTA+ might make it worth it for more people. Anyone with an active subscription also gets access to a selection of Rockstar's other games, including Red Dead Redemption and GTA 5. Of course, you might not have time for any of those until you finish a campaign that can run 80 hours, but the library does make the $8 subscription much easier to justify.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.
    • Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.

    Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

    Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

    Recent findings suggest that “So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” notes Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

    Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

    According to recent reports, passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

    Sources indicate that “It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

    Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

    Recent findings suggest that moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

    Recent findings suggest that as of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

    It has been revealed that the Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

    Sources indicate that dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

    Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

    Sources indicate that yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

    Industry observers note that particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

    At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

    Recent findings suggest that iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”.

    It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

    Recent findings suggest that oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he mentioned.

    Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit.
    • Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's fresh political generation and its giant neighbour.
    • It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit.

    Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's fresh political generation and its giant neighbour.

    It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

    The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

    The talks are expected to cover a broad range of challenges, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

    The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

    India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

    Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

    Nepal suffered devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands missing.

    But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.

    Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

    "The latest Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.

    "They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.

    Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.

    Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them â the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN â UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).

    Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.

    Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.

    But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.

    The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

    According to recent reports, bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.

    India and Nepal share an open border and longstanding economic ties.

    Recent findings suggest that one key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

    Recent findings suggest that "India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.

    India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.

    Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

    In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.

    The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

    "I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border concern with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

    Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its latest airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.

    Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

    Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.

    Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.

    Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.

    His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.

    But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

    "Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," claims Dixit.

    Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

    Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

    Sources indicate that while Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

    The unit can also rip audio CDs to digital files and streams via Bluetooth and Auracast. It's a portable device that charges via USB-C. Finally, there's a headphone jack for solo listening.
