    💡 Key Takeaways
    • State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors.
    • California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
    • Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based firm’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors.

    California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

    Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based firm’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

    “The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” mentioned Bonta.

    “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”.

    The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

    Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.

    Megaspeed has stated it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the manufacturer late last year.

    Bonta noted the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

    In a recent development, “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he stated. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”.

    Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

    Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, mentioned the manufacturer had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.

    Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

    Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.

    The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

    It has been revealed that hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.

    AMD remarked the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

    Anthropic rival indicates companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.
    • That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.
    • Four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.

    That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

    Four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. The Bay Area-based outfit specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion.

    Recent findings suggest that fireworks co-founder Chenyu Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.

    Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

    According to recent reports, notion states AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.

    Fireworks, which is backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, among other firms, was assigned a $17.5 billion valuation in summer. It’s reportedly in early talks for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

    Industry observers note that there’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have confirmed massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.

    Industry observers note that zhao and I spoke onstage about all of it on Thursday at Slush. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say, edited for length and clarity.

    Sources indicate that you spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?

    In a recent development, when you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.

    How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

    It has been revealed that I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.

    How far behind are open models right now?

    Recent findings suggest that A few years ago I’d have mentioned a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.

    If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

    Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 consumers and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.

    In a recent development, in July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

    According to recent reports, we think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

    In a recent development, anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

    On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.

    Industry observers note that fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

    Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.

    Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?

    In a recent development, I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.

    How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

    Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.

    In a recent development, jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?

    Industry observers note that it’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron [Nvidia’s family of open AI models], and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

    Here is a roundup of the main headlines from India on Saturday, November 21 and Sunday, November 22:.

    Workers of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC), the youth wing of the opposition Indian National Congress, protested at US tech giant Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram on Friday, demanding that the group's leaders' Instagram accounts be restored.

    Sources indicate that in Hyderabad, protesters entered the building, smashed plants and clashed with police, according to footage the IYC released. Meta declined to comment.

    The IYC remarked Instagram withheld the accounts of its president and in-charge on November 19 "on BJP orders," referring to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and restored both shortly after the protests.

    Manu Jain, who runs the group's social media, told Reuters thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.

    BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari mentioned: "Congress is a party of goons! Goons of Indian Youth Congress are not only vandalized and destroyed Meta's office in Hyderabad, & also are flaunting it on social media!".

    Meanwhile, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav warned foreign companies against getting involved in Indian politics.

    The Indian government says it orders takedowns only for content that breaches local laws or threatens public safety or national security. In February, it cut the deadline for removing unlawful content from 36 hours to three.

    Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the previous six months, saying most were cases where local law required it to restrict content proactively.

    Earlier this month, Brazil’s top electoral court fined Meta's Facebook $1.3 million for failing to comply with judicial orders during the country's presidential election runoff campaign. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's team accused the company of political bias.

    India closed day three of the first Test against Fresh Zealand on 486-4, a lead of 118 runs. KL Rahul made 136, Shubman Gill 98 and Rishabh Pant was unbeaten on 55 as every one of India's top five passed 50.

    Rahul reached his 13th Test hundred off 207 balls, batting for more than eight hours and sharing stands of 165 with Devdutt Padikkal (80) and 91 with Gill. It completed a set of Test centuries in every major Test-playing nation outside the subcontinent for the Indian wicketkeeper-batsman.

    "It feels really awesome, actually, to be able to achieve something like that," Rahul noted.

    In a recent development, he survived an LBW appeal on 5 that was given not out and Newly introduced Zealand chose not to review. "Those 15 seconds were probably the slowest 15 seconds of my life," he said of the review process.

    Industry observers note that gill and Pant added 100 in the final session before Gill was bowled by Jacob Duffy just before stumps. Duffy finished with 1-180 from 29 overs, the fourth most expensive figures in New Zealand's Test history, AFP remarked.

    The pitch, green on day one, flattened out. "We expected a lot of grass on the wicket, we expected a lot of movement and it has probably not panned out that way," Padikkal said.

    New Zealand were all out for 368 in their first innings.

    The two-match series ends next week in Christchurch.

    At least 14 people have died and more than 200 have been hospitalized after drinking suspected adulterated liquor in Manipur's Chandel district.

    At least 12 people remain in critical condition, local media reported.

    The victims drank the liquor in the Chakpikarong area, about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from the state capital city of Imphal, and deaths were reported between November 18 and 20.

    Sources indicate that chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited the hospitals where most patients were being treated on Friday. He ordered an inquiry and said the culprits would be arrested soon.

    Police said the liquor came from Sugnu in neighboring Kakching district, with no known local brewing in Chandel. A case has been filed, and two people have been arrested.

    The local administration has advised residents not to drink liquor from questionable sources and asked anyone who consumed liquor from the same source to get a medical check-up, even without symptoms.

    Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

    "I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he noted in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.

    Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited Gupta in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.

    Gupta paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.

    Prosecutors also said Gupta had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.

    His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.

    "There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she stated. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.

    According to recent reports, india denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. New Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.

    Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and mentioned outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay.".

    #70368. What are the actual differences between cheap and expensive sound systems?

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    What are the actual differences between cheap and expensive sound systems?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Spending more doesn't guarantee a better fit for you, though there are some clear differences as you climb in price.
    • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
    • Recent findings suggest that your TV's built-in speakers are fine...
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Spending more doesn't guarantee a better fit for you, though there are some clear differences as you climb in price.

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Recent findings suggest that your TV's built-in speakers are fine... if you don't care about hearing dialogue clearly, feeling the bass or knowing where an explosion is coming from. Even an inexpensive soundbar can make a noticeable difference.

    Industry observers note that soundbars can range from around $100 to well over $1,000, as demonstrated by our picks for the best soundbars. Many highly rated models that provide good value fall between $200 and $600 in our findings, as well as those from other outlets like Consumer Reports. The options vary considerably in how they handle surround sound, from basic bars designed to improve dialogue to more elaborate systems with wireless subwoofers and rear speakers.

    According to recent reports, diminishing returns are key here. The biggest improvements usually come from moving beyond TV speakers and entry-level soundbars. After that, you're paying for more capable hardware, additional features and refinements that may be less noticeable to the average listener. Let's look at a couple of different price buckets, which aren't exact quality dividers but will give you an idea.

    A basic soundbar can make dialogue easier to hear and give movies more presence. Models under $100 are pretty stripped-down and have limited connectivity, fewer sound modes and can't reproduce deep bass. They're designed to improve everyday TV audio without needing a complicated setup.

    In a recent development, at this price, you're typically looking at a 2.0 or 2.1 setup. If you're not familiar with speaker channel numbers, a 2.0 soundbar has two audio channels (stereo), while a 2.1 model adds a separate subwoofer to handle lower frequencies. The Hisense HS2100, for example, sells for around $120 and includes a wireless subwoofer that gives it a fuller sound than a standalone bar.

    Recent findings suggest that for just under $200, you can get considerably more hardware. The Hisense HS5100 is a 5.1-channel system (adding two rear speakers and a center channel compared to 2.1) with a dedicated subwoofer and satellite speakers. Instead of relying on processing to simulate surround sound, the rear speakers provide audio behind you. It doesn't support Dolby Atmos, though, so you don't get overhead effects.

    It has been revealed that this is where soundbars start offering more impressive improvements to your TV's audio. You should see features like eARC for sending audio to your soundbar from any other input, as well as Wi-Fi streaming and more robust app features like full EQ management. You might also get upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos, making compatible movie soundtracks more immersive. Exact features vary among models; for example, the Hisense AX3120Q is a 3.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar for around $280.

    Sources indicate that A 3.1.2 system has three front-facing channels, a subwoofer and two height channels. That gives you a dedicated center channel for dialogue and hardware designed to reproduce overhead effects. The Polk Signa S4 is another example for around $449, while Sony's Bravia Theater Bar 5 offers a less expensive $350 alternative with a dedicated subwoofer and 3.1-channel configuration, virtualizing the overhead and directional effects. Neither gives you separate rear speakers for physical surround sound.

    According to recent reports, at the upper end of this price range, there are more complete surround systems with dedicated rear speakers and multiple height channels. The Hisense AX5140Q is a 5.1.4-channel system with a wireless subwoofer, two satellite speakers and four upward-firing drivers. It also includes features like a graphic equalizer, independent channel adjustments and dialogue enhancement. That's a lot more hardware than you'll find in a basic soundbar.

    In a recent development, in this range, you'll find more capable surround sound systems, but the improvements aren't just about adding more speakers. The Samsung HW-Q800F offers 5.1.2-channel audio with a wireless subwoofer and up-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos. It doesn't include rear speakers, though; it uses side-firing drivers for virtual surround effects. Other models, like Samsung's 3.1.2-channel HW-QS700F soundbar, offer features like automatic adjustments based on whether the bar is on a TV stand or a wall.

    The JBL Bar 1000MK2 offers another step up. Its 7.1.4-channel configuration includes detachable, battery-powered satellite speakers, a subwoofer and upward-firing drivers. It also has room correction and a graphic equalizer. The detachable speakers give you physical surround sound when you want it, without having to keep them out permanently.

    At the upper end of this range, you have systems like Marshall's $1,000 Dolby Atmos Heston 120 soundbar. But spending more doesn't necessarily mean getting a better fit for your room.

    Sources indicate that A dedicated home theater system gives you more control over where sound comes from. Instead of using a soundbar to simulate surround effects, an AV receiver sends audio to individual speakers around your room. A basic 5.1 setup includes left and right front speakers, a center channel, two rear surround speakers and a subwoofer.

    In a recent development, the difference isn't just about having more speakers, though. A properly configured surround system can create a more convincing sense of space and make it easier to hear where dialogue and sound effects are coming from. But the difference between surround sound systems and soundbars shows with tradeoffs in cost, space and setup complexity.

    Sources indicate that if you're willing to invest in separate components, a receiver-based system gives you more room to customize and upgrade later. Home Audio Advice put together a roughly $1,300 setup using a Yamaha RX-V4A receiver and a Klipsch Reference Cinema 5.1.4 speaker package. The receiver powers a basic 5.1 setup and the Klipsch package includes four additional height-effect speakers that can be used after upgrading to a compatible receiver. The flexibility is a major advantage.

    In a recent development, however, soundbars are still able to offer a convincing surround experience. Samsung's 11.1.4-channel HW-Q990D soundbar is an example, though it doesn't come cheap. There are also modular options like LG's Dolby Atmos FlexConnect home theater system, which let you arrange compatible speakers around your room without committing to traditional wired placement.

    One of the biggest differences between inexpensive and premium speakers is how accurately they portray the sound captured by media creators. A speaker with an uneven response may emphasize certain frequencies while making others harder to hear, while a more balanced frequency response produces a more natural sound.

    In a recent development, bass reproduction is another area where better equipment makes a noticeable difference. Low-frequency extension describes how deep a bass signal a speaker can play before it starts dropping off. Smaller speakers struggle with the lowest frequencies, which is why a subwoofer makes such a difference in a home theater.

    Sources indicate that louder isn't necessarily better, but a system able to maintain sound quality at higher volume definitely matters. More capable speakers can deliver greater output while maintaining a more consistent sound, which is helpful in larger rooms or when listening at high volumes.

    The jump from TV speakers to an inexpensive soundbar is usually a lot more noticeable than moving from a midrange to a premium one. Even soundbars under $300 can give a substantial improvement, and some budget models deliver sound quality that competes with more expensive options. Consumer Reports has found that certain less expensive soundbars rival pricier models in overall sound quality. Spending more isn't pointless, but the improvements become less direct as you move up the price ladder.

    According to recent reports, at higher price points, you're typically paying for refinements instead of a completely different audio experience. Those improvements can matter if you have a large space, watch a lot of movies, are a serious gamer or want to customize your setup over time. But someone watching content that doesn't take advantage of modern audio features (like news and sports) in a small living room may not notice enough of a difference to justify doubling their budget.

    According to recent reports, your room can also limit the benefits of expensive equipment. Walls, floors, furniture and speaker placement all affect how sound travels, especially at lower frequencies. Before spending hundreds on new equipment, try repositioning your speakers or changing where you sit; small changes to your audio setup can pay off.

    If you're looking for clearer dialogue and better everyday TV audio, you probably don't need to spend more than $150 to $200. A basic 2.1 soundbar gives you fuller sound and deeper bass without taking up much space. Inexpensive soundbars will work particularly well in small and medium-sized rooms, which makes them a practical choice if you aren't looking for a full home theater experience.

    In a recent development, if you watch a lot of movies or listen to music through your TV, spending around $250 to $500 gives you more options. This is where you can start finding dedicated center channels, Wi-Fi streaming and, depending on the model, physical rear speakers or Dolby Atmos.

    Spending $500 to $1,000 or more makes sense if you want a more complete home theater experience, have a larger room or care about getting the most out of movies, games and music. At this level, you can find high-quality soundbars with multiple height channels, room correction and more customization options. You can also start building a component-based system, giving you more flexibility to upgrade over time.

    Recent findings suggest that just remember that a higher price doesn't automatically mean a better fit. Consider your room, listening habits and the features you'll actually use before deciding how much to spend.

    The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

    Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:.

    It has been revealed that the pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

    CTIA mentioned the pilot test demonstrates “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”.

    In a recent development, the FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”.

    The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

    Carr noted that “contraband cell phones continue to pour into prisons by the thousands each year,” with “estimates indicat[ing] that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices.” He said the phones have been used to plan scams, drug trafficking, and violent attacks.

    “In Georgia, an incarcerated gang leader directed a drive-by shooting that killed two 13-year-old boys at a birthday party,” Carr said, referring to a 2024 shooting.

    Carr defended the plan against criticism that it will block legitimate communications outside the prisons, saying it includes safeguards to prevent that.

    In a recent development, “Those that want to use the technology will apply to the FCC, explain how they plan to deploy it, and show through testing that it stays inside the designated area and doesn’t interfere with lawful communications outside the prison walls,” Carr mentioned. “Communities nearby will receive notice before operations start. We’re also seeking comment on next steps, including ways to close remaining loopholes on other frequencies and the possibility of quiet zones around correctional facilities.”.

    Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern said the FCC should have considered the benefits of contraband phones being used to document abuses inside prisons.

    According to recent reports, “Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country and people wishing to expose abuses and inhumane conditions from the inside often do not have many options,” Stern wrote in a letter to FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez’s office, which was included on the FCC docket. “Last year’s Oscar-nominated film, The Alabama Solution, used footage incarcerated people captured with contraband cell phones to show Americans some of the awful things that go on in state prisons that they’d have no other way of seeing. The same footage bolstered an ongoing DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons and was crucial evidence in a civil lawsuit by Steven Davis, who was brutally killed by prison guards, that eventually settled.”.

    Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by prison phone companies ViaPath (aka Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, the National District Attorneys Association, the Correctional Leaders Association, and National Association of Police Organizations.

    “Inmates have used these phones to coordinate attacks against correctional officers and their families, as well as inmate violence, strikes, disturbances, and full-scale riots,” the National Association of Police Organizations mentioned. “They also use contraband phones to organize deliveries of illegal drugs and weapons into correctional facilities. These dangers underscore the need to authorize indoor jamming in state and local correctional facilities.”.

    Gomez, the only Democrat on the three-member commission, stated she’s concerned about potential unintended consequences, but voted with Republicans to allow jamming after safeguards were added to the order.

    “For the last 90 years, the Federal Communications Commission has prohibited jamming by non-federal actors and even prohibited jamming equipment to be introduced into the American market,” Gomez remarked. “That is because jamming devices are specifically designed to interfere with communications devices in order to render them un-usable.”.

    Gomez mentioned that “jamming can prevent devices from completing 911 and emergency calls as well as interfere with communications networks used by fire, police, Emergency Medical Services, and other public safety entities.” She also said making jamming equipment available in the American market could lead to “unauthorized sale of this hazardous equipment,” and that “the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise.” Criminals have used “Wi-Fi jammers to disrupt security systems, security cameras, and cellphones to conduct robberies at homes and at stores,” she said.

    Gomez said she’s glad the final order includes safeguards “to ensure that jamming is contained to this unique use, to permit jamming by a very limited category of authorized actors, and to take as much care as possible to prevent jamming and jamming equipment from becoming a hazard to safety.”.

    Gomez partially dissented because she is worried the FCC will let correctional facilities and prison phone companies charge higher prices for inmate calling services that connect inmates with family members. Under US law, the FCC sets limits on those prices and considers prisons’ and jails’ safety and security costs when deciding how much money they can charge, she said.

    Industry observers note that gomez said, “While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures… Jamming is specifically designed to block communications and is certainly not necessary to provide phone and video calls for incarcerated individuals. We should have made this clear in today’s order. Because we failed to do so, I dissent in part.”.

    According to recent reports, the FCC order could be challenged in court. The CTIA has argued that the FCC “has no authority to allow jamming” under the Communications Act, which directs the FCC to prevent interference.

    According to recent reports, AT&T remarked the FCC’s legal justification “is premised on a fundamental factual error: the assumption that jammers will only block ‘unauthorized’ communications without impacting lawful uses. There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others. That is because radio jammers ‘block all wireless communications on affected spectrum bands,’ and, as the FCC has noted in the past, ‘cannot differentiate between contraband devices and legitimate devices.’”.

    In a recent development, AT&T said that “there is simply no way to limit the reach of jammers to the confines of a given facility. Jammers have been shown to cause interference outside the facilities in which they operate, greatly increasing the risk that someone living or traveling nearby will be impacted.”.

    • Donald Trump has stated he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
    • "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US.

    Donald Trump has stated he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

    "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

    Data centres were a central glitch in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

    Sources indicate that tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

    "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

    "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen.".

    But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

    "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

    Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

    It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

    Washington on Monday declared firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

    The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

    Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back.

    Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

    As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

    Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

    According to recent reports, "You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

    According to recent reports, "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets.".

    Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

    Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

    The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

    In September Google revealed a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

    Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

    Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

    Google has been contacted for comment.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout.

    Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

    As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

    Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

    Recent findings suggest that shares in the frontier AI firm behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

    In a recent development, anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

    It has been revealed that US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

    Sources indicate that neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that demonstrates no sign of easing just yet.”.

    Industry observers note that global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in significant chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

    The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

    Sources indicate that in Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

    Sources indicate that european stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

    The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

    Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

    “The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp noted.

    Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

    Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, remarked: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

    “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”.

    Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

    Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

    Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

    Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

    #70362. Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO

    Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, anthropic became a public manufacturer on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders.
    • At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes.
    • Sources indicate that anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, anthropic became a public manufacturer on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

    At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

    Sources indicate that anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The organization said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

    Recent findings suggest that however, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The firm points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”.

    With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

    $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

    Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

    Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

    Industry observers note that 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a major stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

    The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.

    Recent findings suggest that more than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

    Industry observers note that anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

    All told, the firm has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

    #70360. Industry News: How to use Gemini Notebook to turn your research into an interactive site

    Industry News: How to use Gemini Notebook to turn your research into an interactive site

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All you have to do is tell Gemini to make you a site using your sources.
    • It has been revealed that google's tagline for Gemini Notebook is "understand anything," because it's meant to help you better understand difficult concepts by creating study guides and even podcasts.
    • In a recent development, to use the service, tap or click on Create notebook and then upload your sources for any particular topic.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All you have to do is tell Gemini to make you a site using your sources.

    It has been revealed that google's tagline for Gemini Notebook is "understand anything," because it's meant to help you better understand difficult concepts by creating study guides and even podcasts. Before it was called the Gemini Notebook, it was known as Google NotebookLM, which the organization presented as its "deep research tool.".

    In a recent development, to use the service, tap or click on Create notebook and then upload your sources for any particular topic. It accepts different types of sources, such as PDFs and images from your device or your Google Drive account. It also accepts links to websites, open source textbooks, books from the Play store and even copied text, such as your notes or emails. Gemini Notebook will then use those sources to create what you need, whether it's a study guide or a podcast featuring two AI hosts.

    It has been revealed that gemini Notebook's latest feature can create a website you can interact with. Every website it makes has a unique design and comes with various elements, such as clickable sections, flash cards and quizzes that test whether you've learned anything from the information presented in it.

    According to recent reports, it's incredibly easy to create an interactive site with Gemini Notebook. At the moment, the feature is live on desktop and available for all owners 18 years old and above. It is coming soon to the service's mobile app. But for now, you have to visit Gemini Notebook on the web and then hit Upcoming Notebook or Create notebook.

    Sources indicate that in the chat box within the newly introduced notebook's interface, type "make me a site" along with instructions on what you want the service to create for you. For the example above, I wrote: "Make a me site to help me understand the solar system and its elements. Explain them to me in simple sections with flash cards and create a quiz at the end." It will then draw information from your sources to make the website for you.

    If you don't have any sources uploaded, it will ask you if you want to do a web search to find the information you need. It could be good enough if you want to learn about known concepts and don't need the website to reflect details and data only you have access to. Gemini will let you know if your interactive site is done. You'll then be able to access the site in the Studio panel on the right-hand side of your screen. Just click or tap on the tab to load the site.

    In my case, Gemini created a colorful website, with illustrations of the solar system and clickable sections, as you can see in the image above. Clicking on Mercury, for instance, shows a card with information about the smallest planet in our Solar System. It made separate sections for the four inner terrestrial planets, including Earth, and for the gas and ice giants in the outer Solar System. There are more clickable sections for the asteroid belt, the Kuiper belt and Oort cloud.

    Maybe you read that last sentence and thought: "the? what?? cloud???" and rightly so! The Oort cloud is an entirely theoretical cluster of small, icy bodies past the Kuiper belt. Gemini presented it on this website as if it were extant and observed, describing it as "the home of long-period comets." The Kuiper belt was theorized decades before it was confirmed; that might end up being the case with the Oort cloud too. As with anything AI though, Gemini is not only capable of both hallucinating but of confidently misstating things too.

    It has been revealed that in addition to creating easy-to-digest interactive websites to help you learn or prepare for exams, you can also use the upcoming feature for other purposes.     • President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and claims he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi.
    • Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the proposal.
    • In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and claims he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi.

    Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the proposal.

    In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

    Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

    At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

    Recent findings suggest that “We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he remarked.

    He remarked Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

    “You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he remarked.

    “We want them to build it here.”.

    With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

    The Trump administration on Monday issued fresh rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

    China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

    In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and mentioned: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”.

    Industry observers note that he added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”.

    Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump mentioned the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

    Sources indicate that “I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president mentioned. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”.

    Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

    Industry observers note that “I can’t speak to America,” he noted, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”.

    He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

    “I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he stated.

    In a recent development, trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He remarked Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”.

    Industry observers note that and he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”.

    #70354. NASA’s fresh Moon initiative is taking shape, but some major questions remain

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2287 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    NASA’s fresh Moon initiative is taking shape, but some major questions remain

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.
    • For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships.
    • In a recent development, early next year, SpaceX intends to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

    For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

    In a recent development, early next year, SpaceX intends to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

    The Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.

    Industry observers note that other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.

    Ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.

    Recent findings suggest that for Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a Fresh Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.

    Then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

    NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.

    So, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a big reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.

    “The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech remarked. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.

    According to recent reports, “With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech mentioned. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”.

    Sources indicate that artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.

    “I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech stated. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”.

    The Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.

    “With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech noted. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”.

    While there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a new milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.

    Sources indicate that NASA levied newly introduced test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The manufacturer intends to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.

    “One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech said. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.

    This year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight initiative for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated intends will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion.

    Recent findings suggest that “Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech remarked. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”.

    The fresh concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.

    Industry observers note that “One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech said. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”.

    The six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.

    Now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.

    According to recent reports, what’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.

    It has been revealed that “We’re still working that out,” Creech said. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”.

    According to recent reports, for missions using Blue Moon, the lander will connect with Orion in orbit around the Moon. Blue Origin’s updated intends do away with the requirement for in-space refueling but will still require four introduces of the company’s Newly introduced Glenn rocket, one for the Blue Moon lander itself and three with transfer stages to boost it out of Earth orbit to the Moon.

    A new stretched Centaur upper stage for the Space Launch System should give the rocket energy to send Orion to low-lunar orbit, which it could not reach with the current version of SLS. NASA has not determined if the new Centaur exploration stage will be ready in time for Artemis IV. If not, Artemis IV could fly with the last of NASA’s in-stock SLS upper stages.

    According to recent reports, NASA is also waiting to decide which lander to use on Artemis IV. In either case, two of Orion’s four astronauts will transfer into the landers for the final descent to the lunar surface for a four-day stay, then take off and return to Orion.

    Recent findings suggest that starship and Blue Moon must each complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. The landing demos are targeted for late 2027 or early 2028, Creech noted, but they won’t necessarily test everything crews will need when they head for the lunar south pole.

    According to recent reports, starship’s elevator, for example, is not part of SpaceX’s uncrewed landing demonstration. Engineers will use a test lab at Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama to check the elevator’s performance in a simulated lunar environment.

    According to recent reports, NASA did not initially require SpaceX or Blue Origin to prove their landers could take off from the Moon before a crew mission. Government officials later added the lunar takeoff requirement for each organization’s uncrewed landing demos.

    For now, NASA is leaving the details of the uncrewed takeoff demo up to SpaceX and Blue Origin. During Apollo, NASA’s lunar lander never landed on the Moon before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. NASA did, however, fly a dress rehearsal around the Moon on Apollo 10 that included a test of the lunar module’s landing abort capability.

    “Where we are today is, Blue will land and then do a full ascent back to the rendezvous point with Orion,” Creech stated. “With SpaceX. They will land, they will take off again, get to main stage on the engines, and then they will do another landing on the surface.”.

    That could change. Today’s initiative gives SpaceX two shots at proving Starship can safely land on the Moon, but it comes with trade-offs.

    In a recent development, “When I came into the program, I was like, ‘Why are we not going all the way to the rendezvous point?’” said Creech, who took over as HLS program manager in 2025. “Some of my key people felt strongly we would get more out of the way we’re doing it now. There are others that have different opinions… We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”.

    In a recent development, for Starship, orbital refueling remains the key to the Moon. SpaceX’s propellant transfer demonstration will involve two Starships, one launched from Florida and another from Texas, docking together in low-Earth orbit and transferring a “meaningful” amount of propellant from one ship to the other, Creech said.

    “The first quarter of next year, we will see a long-awaited propellant transfer test from SpaceX, where they launch two Starships in pretty close proximity, actually dock, and transfer, we’re calling it a meaningful amount, of propellant,” Creech told Ars. “That is going to be a big learning point if they pull that off, because their architecture depends on propellant aggregation and multiple propellant flights.”.

    The propellant transfer test will mark the first time one spacecraft has offloaded a significant quantity of cryogenic propellants—in this case, methane and liquid oxygen—onto another vehicle in space. It is the culmination of decades of government and commercial research on cryogenic orbital refueling. The results will tell engineers how much of the propellant will be lost from boil-off during the transfer.

    Recent findings suggest that that is one reason why there’s still so much ambiguity about how many Starship refueling tankers SpaceX will need to launch to give the Starship lunar lander enough gas to fly to the Moon. Without refueling, Starships are restricted to flights in low-Earth orbit.

    The low end of the estimate for Starship tankers is six to eight refueling flights to support a Starship lunar mission. Those numbers come from Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, and fall below NASA’s own conservative planning figure of 20 refueling launches. Musk’s figures hinge on future Starship upgrades to reach the vehicle’s full potential. SpaceX’s goal is to get Starship’s lift capacity up to 100 to 200 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit. Today’s version of Starship, known as Starship V3, is still far short of 100 metric tons of payload capacity.

    For context, a Starship carries 1,600 metric tons of propellant with its tanks full. Refueling flights using future, fully optimized Starships might be able to fill those tanks with as few as six tankers. That is not the case today.

    SpaceX is working on a taller, heavier Starship called Starship V4. It will fly with nine Raptor engines, an upgrade over the six-engine variant flying today. In 2025, Musk said Starship V4’s first launch was targeted for 2027. There hasn’t been a recent enhancement to the schedule for Starship V4.

    The initial Artemis lunar missions will use Starship V3, Creech stated.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

    The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”.

    “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting states. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”.

    The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”.

    TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

    Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have introduced such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the fresh John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

    Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

    It has been revealed that the outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging owners from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

    Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
